agents.brief: Explore KCNE1 function/expression DMS prediction. Find a robust, simple validation-tested model using only public training data; run evidence only with lab exec, publish a prediction-test contribution if justified, and share artifact/blob IDs and key caveats.

Explore RASK_HUMAN Weng abundance and DARPin K55 datasets for a robust held-out-prediction contribution. Use lab exec for all evidence; publish only if validation supports it and report artifact/blob IDs and caveats.
Explore Firnberg/Stiffler BLAT DMS for a robust prediction contribution; use lab exec for evidence, publish if supported, and report artifact/blob IDs and caveats.
Explore CASP3 DMS for a defensible held-out-prediction contribution. Use lab exec for evidence; publish if supported, report IDs and caveats.

Independently test whether adding the paired KCNE1 assay improves prediction beyond the accepted mutation-feature models for both expression and function. Use only lab exec evidence, use identical held-out folds, inspect/fetch accepted work, and if warranted publish a material extension or refutation consuming the prior model code. Include an evaluator held-out test.

Challenge the accepted paired-assay BLAT findings: assess mutation/variant leakage, exact-match coverage, and validation protocol. Compare isotonic transfer and sequence-plus-auxiliary ridge fairly, ideally with variant/site grouped validation and held-out prediction test. Build materially on prior accepted BLAT work and use lab exec evidence only.

Independently test robustness of accepted CASP3 position-conditioned mutation features and the founder physicochemical extension, especially position-grouped splits, feature coding and nested tuning. Consume accepted code in lab exec; publish a substantive correction/extension only if supported, with evaluator held-out test.

Independently build on findin-db70a492 and accepted KCNE1 expression findings. Reproduce site-held-out comparisons, investigate whether the modest expression interaction gain over one-hot survives a stronger equally tuned baseline or alternative site partitions. Run evidence only through lab exec, publish only numbers recorded by exec, and materially extend/correct/refute the accepted work if warranted. Use remaining session time efficiently.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay calibration improves Firnberg BLAT fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: In shuffled five-fold cross-validation, I calibrated Firnberg target scores from the matched Stiffler assay measurements with isotonic regression. Calibration uses only target labels in each training fold; the opposite-assay train.csv is treated as available auxiliary data. The predictor substantially reduces MAE in this validation. Important caveat: this result depends on availability of measurements for matching variants in the other assay, and random folds of the provided train set are not an independent experimental replication. The evaluator test applies the same procedure to held-out Firnberg inputs.

artifacts.title: BLAT transfer gains depend on exact cross-assay variant availability
artifacts.summary: I extend the accepted BLAT cross-assay calibration result with fold-matched residue-grouped validation and a direct comparison to sequence-plus-auxiliary ridge. On both target assays, isotonic calibration of exact-matched source scores beats auxiliary ridge when the held-out variant's source score is available. When those test-variant scores are masked, isotonic falls back to sequence-only ridge and the ridge with a missingness feature does not improve on that baseline. Thus the strong paired-assay result is evidence for transfer on variants already measured in the source assay, not generalization to variants lacking source measurements. The comparison selects auxiliary-ridge regularization only within outer training folds and uses the same outer folds for both arms. The held-out test compares isotonic transfer with sequence-ridge fallback against sequence-plus-auxiliary ridge; it uses public source-assay training scores only for exact matching sequences.

I’ll test two defensible routes against the exact ridge baseline: regularization/feature changes within an assay, and transfer from the paired assay on the same protein. I’ll use repeated random validation splits and record the results through `lab exec`.

I’ll test the strongest plausible simple signal first: cross-assay transfer for the same mutation, calibrated using only target-assay training variants, with the one-hot ridge baseline as fallback. Random held-out mutations will reveal whether sibling-assay public measurements help beyond sequence features.

I’ll benchmark the evaluator’s ridge baseline against tuned regularization and a cross-assay feature, using repeated 25% validation splits so withheld-variant coverage in the paired KRAS assays can be measured directly.

Because hidden variants are likely substitutions at positions represented in training, I’ll compare the provided ridge baseline with mutation-property models under five-fold random variant splits. I’ll also measure a position-held-out split as a stricter generalization check, since the public data covers nearly every site.

The two assays share nearly all measured mutations and their scores are strongly correlated, so I’ll test a cross-assay calibrated predictor against sequence ridge using held-out target-assay folds. This uses the other assay as auxiliary training data, not held-out target labels.

The first cross-validation run suggests position-specific physicochemical features may help, but the margin over the baseline is small. I’ll compare several mutation encodings on identical folds and report their paired errors before selecting a model for the held-out prediction test.

Cross-assay measurements appear weakly related, so I won’t use them. I’ll broaden the validation to additive mutation encodings—site, amino-acid, and physicochemical effects—against the exact baseline, and select only using repeated training-data splits.

I’ll measure how often each assay’s mutations are present in the other assay and compare simple cross-assay calibration variants under the same folds, so the prediction test’s expected coverage and method choice are grounded in evidence.

The leading model encodes position and position-specific alternative amino acid, with global wild-type and alternative amino-acid effects. To check that its advantage isn’t a lucky split, I’ll compare it against the specified ridge baseline across repeated random folds, and retain position-held-out results as a harder generalization diagnostic.

The paired-assay results look promising, especially for BLAT, but evaluation must have access to the auxiliary assay’s public measurements at test time. I’ll inspect the test schema and retrieve complete run records before publishing anything.

The previous transfer estimate used source-assay labels for mutations held out in the target folds, which would not be available for genuinely hidden variants. I’m replacing it with a leakage-safe stacked predictor: cross-fitted source-assay ridge predictions calibrate to target scores, and held-out predictions use only source labels from the training fold.
